title: Bridal Poses: 24 Wedding Dress Poses With Angles and Lenses — cv.cm
description: 24 bridal poses in one table with how to do each, the best camera angle and lens, plus veil, train, bouquet, sitting, looking-back and ring close-up poses.
h1: What are the best poses for bridal photos?
answer: The most reliable bridal poses are the three-quarter stand (body at 45 degrees, face to camera), the over-the-shoulder look back, a slow walk, the bouquet held at navel height, a seated pose with the dress spread, and veil shots in the wind. Keep weight on the back leg, elbows off the waist, hands soft, and the camera near waist height for full-length frames.

sections.h: The five rules behind every bridal pose
body: Most bridal poses are variations of a few body rules. Learn these and you can fix any pose that looks stiff.

ol: Angle the body. Turn the hips and shoulders about 45 degrees from the camera, then turn the face back. Straight-on looks wide and formal.
Weight on the back leg. Bend the front knee slightly. Even under a long skirt, this tilts the hips and drops one shoulder, which looks relaxed.
Space between arms and waist. A small gap shows the waistline of the dress. Arms pressed to the body look wider.
Chin forward and slightly down. This defines the jaw. A raised chin from a low camera makes the face look rounder.
Soft hands. Fingers slightly curved, touching lightly. Gripping hands look tense.

body: Camera height matters as much as the pose. For full-length shots, hold the camera at about waist height so the body is not shortened. For close-ups, the camera can be at eye level or slightly above.

sections.h: 24 bridal poses with angle and lens
body: Lens lengths are full-frame equivalents. On a phone, 1x is roughly 24 to 26 mm, 2x is roughly 48 to 52 mm, and 3x is roughly 70 to 77 mm, depending on the phone.

body: For the same framing, stand about 1.7 times as far away with an 85 mm lens as with a 50 mm lens (85 divided by 50). For pictures of these body positions, see cv.cm's pose reference (standing, sitting, leaning and looking-back poses, and camera angles).
A veil is light and sheer, so it photographs best with light coming through it from the side or behind. Front light makes it almost invisible.

ul: Wind: stand side-on to the wind. Take many frames with burst; the veil shape changes every half second.
No wind: a helper stands out of frame, lifts the veil and lets it go on a count of three. Shoot at 1/500 s or faster to freeze it.

Over the face: pull the veil forward, look down, then slowly lift the eyes. Focus on the eye nearest the camera, not the fabric. On a phone, tap the eye; if the camera keeps focusing on the veil, move a little closer or farther and tap again.
Framing through the veil: the photographer stands behind the bride and shoots through the edge of the veil for a soft white frame.
Long cathedral veil: spread it on the ground in a straight line behind you and shoot from a high angle.

sections.h: Dress train, bouquet and sitting poses
body: Train: before each frame, lift the train with both hands, give it a small shake and let it fall in a curve. Check that it is not folded under itself. For a full train shot, use a wider lens (24 to 35 mm) so the whole curve fits.

Bouquet: hold it with both hands at navel height with the elbows slightly out, or with one hand at hip height. A bouquet held at the chest hides the bodice and looks like a shield. Tilt the top of the bouquet a little towards the camera so the flowers face the lens.

Sitting: sit on the front third of the seat, back straight, both knees turned to the side away from the camera, ankles together. Place the bouquet in the lap or on the knee. Spread the skirt so its edge makes a smooth curve. On steps, sit sideways and let the dress fall down the steps.

body.note: In a fitted dress, sitting can pull the fabric. Test the sitting pose at the fitting, and bring safety pins in case a seam needs help.

sections.h: Looking back, close-ups, hands and ring
body: The looking-back pose shows the back of the dress, which is often the most detailed part. Turn the back to the camera. Turn the head to the near shoulder, not past it, so the neck does not twist. Drop the near shoulder slightly. Look either at the camera or down at the shoulder.

Close-ups need sharp eyes. Use 85 mm or a phone's 2x or 3x lens, focus on the nearest eye, and use f/2 to f/2.8 for a soft background. Too wide (f/1.2 to f/1.4) at close range can leave the far eye soft.

ul: Hands: show the side of the hand, not the flat back. Fingers slightly apart and curved.
Ring: rest the hand on the bouquet, the dress, or a dark surface. Turn the ring so the stone catches the light.
Rings alone: place them on the bouquet, a flower, a book or the shoes, and use side light from a window.
Phone ring close-up: use the 2x or 3x lens and step back rather than moving the 1x lens very close, which can fail to focus and distorts fingers.

body: Grooms use the same base rules: body angled, weight on the back leg, hands busy. Good groom poses are buttoning the jacket, adjusting cufflinks, hands in pockets with thumbs out, leaning on a wall, and walking. A camera-shy groom can be photographed from behind or in detail shots first.

For couples, the standard poses are the back hug (groom behind the bride, both looking at each other or the camera), the forehead kiss (shot from the side), the walk hand in hand, and the couple looking out at the view with the background filling the frame. The pre-wedding photoshoot guide on this shelf covers couple poses in more detail.

Customs differ. In some cultures couples do not kiss or hug in public photos, and some traditional outfits have their own formal poses, such as a hanbok bow or a kimono stance with the hands folded in front. Ask what feels right before suggesting a pose.

faq.q: How do brides pose with a bouquet?
faq.a: Hold it with both hands at or just below the navel, elbows slightly away from the body, and tilt the flowers towards the camera. For variety, hold it low at one hip with one hand.

faq.q: How do I look natural in wedding photos?
faq.a: Move instead of holding still: walk, turn, adjust the veil or look at the ring. Ask the photographer to use burst so you can pick the frame where your face is relaxed.

faq.q: What angle is most flattering for a bride?
faq.a: For full-length shots, the camera at waist height with the body turned about 45 degrees. For close-ups, the camera at eye level or slightly above, with the chin forward and down.

faq.q: What lens is best for bridal portraits?
faq.a: An 85 mm lens (or a phone's 2x to 3x lens) is a common choice for close and half-body portraits, and 35 to 50 mm (or 1x) for full-length shots and scenes with the venue.

faq.q: How do you pose a bride sitting down?
faq.a: Sit on the front edge of the seat with a straight back, turn both knees away from the camera, keep ankles together, and spread the skirt in a smooth curve.
